sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Independently read the actual AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS (Transact-SQL) receipt. Syntax supplies optional PARAMETERS on an invocation. Arguments says the valid JSON parameters are appended to that call's REST request body; Optional parameters explicitly says a value overrides the matching model-definition parameter at runtime. It uses a model dimensions value of 1536 to illustrate replacement, and Example D passes a JSON dimensions value of 768 on one call. The retry_count example independently describes the same invocation-over-model precedence for another parameter. These establish request construction, not stored-model mutation. The Return types paragraph says a single-column table/JSON while SELECT and UPDATE examples appear scalar; the candidate deliberately asks only which dimension parameter is sent and asserts no return-type shape or executed result.

Independently read Create and manage external models in SQL. It identifies external-model configuration as reusable database metadata, shows PARAMETERS in the created model definition, and states that ALTER EXTERNAL MODEL updates metadata when endpoints, credentials or configuration change. Its later AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS query references the existing model rather than reconfiguring it. Combined with the function reference's per-request runtime override contract, this establishes that a later independent call without PARAMETERS uses the still-stored model default. No source says an invocation itself performs an ALTER. The unit's broad remote-only description is not used to deny the separately documented local Preview runtime.

choiceReviews.rationale: First 1536; later 1536 gets the later default right but ignores the first invocation's explicit dimensions=768 request parameter. The product reference says the supplied value overrides a matching model parameter at runtime. Literal positive countercontext with this exact ordered pair: the stored default is 1536 and neither call supplies a dimensions override, or the first explicitly supplies dimensions=1536 and the second omits it. Then both request bodies use 1536. The candidate instead states a valid 768 override on the first call, so that positive default-preservation context does not apply.

First 768; later 768 incorrectly treats the first request's override as persistent model configuration. PARAMETERS modifies that invocation's request body; model metadata changes are a separate ALTER operation, excluded between these calls. Literal positive countercontext with the exact ordered pair: a model's stored dimensions default is already 768, the first call explicitly requests 768 and the later call omits PARAMETERS. Both requests then use 768. Alternatively both calls could independently override to 768. Neither hypothetical says the first call mutates the default, and both differ from the stated unchanged 1536 default/later omission.

First 768; later 1536 follows the two distinct scopes. The first valid JSON override supplies the dimensions value for that request; the later independent call supplies no override and uses the still-stored 1536 model value. The function reference documents runtime override precedence, and the training unit distinguishes reusable metadata from explicit ALTER changes. Literal confirming context is exactly the stated sequence with a supporting endpoint and no intervening model alteration. This judgment concerns the outgoing dimension parameter only, not whether SQL exposes one vector, a table, JSON text or a particular assignable return type.

First 1536; later 768 reverses which invocation carries the runtime override. Nothing in the documented precedence rule defers the first call's override until a later call. Literal positive countercontext with this exact ordered pair: retain the 1536 model default, have the first invocation omit PARAMETERS, and supply dimensions=768 on the later invocation. Each call then independently follows the same documented default/override rule. The candidate explicitly specifies the opposite placement, so this sourced alternative sequence cannot defend d in the actual stem.
